verses.text: There was a famine in the land, besides the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, to Gerar.
Yahweh appeared to him, and said, “Don’t go down into Egypt. Live in the land I will tell you about.
Live in this land, and I will be with you, and will bless you. For I will give to you, and to your offspring,  all these lands, and I will establish the oath which I swore to Abraham your father.
I will multiply your offspring  as the stars of the sky, and will give all these lands to your offspring.  In your offspring  will all the nations of the earth be blessed,
because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my requirements, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.”
Isaac lived in Gerar.

The men of the place asked him about his wife. He said, “She is my sister,” for he was afraid to say, “My wife”, lest, he thought, “the men of the place might kill me for Rebekah, because she is beautiful to look at.”
When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was caressing Rebekah, his wife.
Abimelech called Isaac, and said, “Behold, surely she is your wife. Why did you say, ‘She is my sister?’” Isaac said to him, “Because I said, ‘Lest I die because of her.’”
Abimelech said, “What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us!”
Abimelech commanded all the people, saying, “He who touches this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”
Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
The man grew great, and grew more and more until he became very great.
He had possessions of flocks, possessions of herds, and a great household. The Philistines envied him.
Now all the wells which his father’s servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped, and filled with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac, “Go from us, for you are much mightier than we.”
Isaac departed from there, encamped in the valley of Gerar, and lived there.

Isaac dug again the wells of water, which they had dug in the days of Abraham his father. For the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham. He called their names after the names by which his father had called them.
Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.
The herdsmen of Gerar argued with Isaac’s herdsmen, saying, “The water is ours.” He called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him.
They dug another well, and they argued over that, also. He called its name Sitnah.
He left that place, and dug another well. They didn’t argue over that one. He called it Rehoboth. He said, “For now Yahweh has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”
He went up from there to Beersheba.

Yahweh appeared to him the same night, and said, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Don’t be afraid, for I am with you, and will bless you, and multiply your offspring  for my servant Abraham’s sake.”
He built an altar there, and called on Yahweh’s name, and pitched his tent there. There Isaac’s servants dug a well.
Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzath his friend, and Phicol the captain of his army.
Isaac said to them, “Why have you come to me, since you hate me, and have sent me away from you?”
They said, “We saw plainly that Yahweh was with you. We said, ‘Let there now be an oath between us, even between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, as we have not touched you, and as we have done to you nothing but good, and have sent you away in peace.’ You are now the blessed of Yahweh.”
He made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
They rose up some time in the morning, and swore to one another. Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.
The same day, Isaac’s servants came, and told him concerning the well which they had dug, and said to him, “We have found water.”
He called it Shibah.  Therefore the name of the city is Beersheba  to this day.
When Esau was forty years old, he took as wife Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
They grieved Isaac’s and Rebekah’s spirits.

footnotes.content: Once more a famine presses the land, and once more the family of promise must choose whether to trust the God who gave them this land. Isaac walks in his father's steps, but he is not merely repeating Abraham—he is learning for himself to look to Yahweh when scarcity tempts him to run elsewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh meets Isaac in the very place where fear would pull him toward Egypt. Before Isaac moves his feet, the Lord speaks a word of restraint: do not go down. How often our greatest rescue is not a new door opened, but an old door closed by the faithful Shepherd.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord anchors Isaac's hope not in his own strength, but in His presence and faithfulness. The oath sworn to Abraham now rests on Isaac, not because of Isaac's worthiness, but because of the God who cannot break His word. That same faithfulness holds every believer in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God promises to multiply Isaac's offspring beyond counting and to bless all nations through them. Here we see the covenant expanding: the blessing of Abraham is not hoarded for his family alone, but is meant to overflow to the ends of the earth. One day that promise finds its yes in Jesus, the true Seed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham's obedience becomes the reason for blessing upon Isaac—a reminder that God faithfully keeps His word across generations. Yet the greater wonder is this: our standing before God rests not on our obedience, but on the perfect obedience of Jesus, to whom every covenant promise points.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple sentence marks quiet faithfulness: Isaac lived in Gerar because he heeded the word of Yahweh. Often the greatest act of trust is not a grand venture, but staying where God has told us to stay, even when fear whispers that another place would be safer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac falls into the same sin as his father, afraid that beauty will cost him his life. Yet notice: the God who called him continues to care for him. Our failures do not undo the covenant faithfulness of the God who has bound Himself to His people in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech looks out his window and sees the truth. What Isaac tried to hide in fear is exposed before the king. God often uses unexpected means to protect His people, and He is never unaware of the schemes meant to do His covenant family harm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac's honest admission—"I said, 'Lest I die because of her'"—reveals a heart gripped by fear rather than trust. How tender that the Lord still protects Rebekah and preserves Isaac, not for their courage, but for the sake of His own promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech rightly sees the potential for guilt: one careless act could have brought judgment on his whole people. There is a kind of conscience here that, though dim, recognizes that God's people are not to be trifled with. The Lord Himself is the shield of those He has called.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king issues a decree of protection over Isaac and Rebekah. Ironically, the very man Isaac feared becomes an instrument of God's mercy. Our God is able to turn the hearts of kings to guard the ones He has promised to bless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In a time of famine, Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold. This is no accident of soil, but the direct fulfillment of Yahweh's word: "I will bless you." When God gives His promise, even barren ground can yield abundance for the sake of those He loves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man grew great by the blessing of God, not by grasping for it. Yet with prosperity comes a new test: will he trust the Giver when the gifts begin to attract envy? The believer learns to enjoy God's blessings as gifts, not as idols to clutch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abundance stirs envy in the Philistines. It is an old story: the world often resents those whom God has blessed. But the security of God's people is never in their possessions—it is in the promise that the God who blessed them still goes with them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They stop up the wells their fathers dug. Envy cannot create, so it seeks to destroy or take what others have received as a gift. How like the enemy of our souls, who cannot quench the living water Christ gives, yet labors to block our access to it in our own hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech politely asks Isaac to leave, for he has become "much mightier than we." Fear often dresses itself in courtesy. Yet the one whom men ask to depart is the one whom Yahweh has commanded to stay in this land—and the God who sent him will provide for him elsewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac departs peacefully, not with an army but with trust in God. When driven from places of blessing by man's envy, the child of promise can move on in peace, knowing his true inheritance is not held by Philistine hands, but secured by God's unshakeable oath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac lovingly reopens the wells his father dug, restoring the names Abraham gave them. There is beauty here: he honors the faith of the previous generation while walking in his own. We too are blessed to drink from wells dug by godly forebears, even as we look to the Fountain of living water Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His servants find a well of springing water—a picture of God's faithful provision breaking through again. The Lord who led them to leave is the same Lord who leads them to find water in the valley. He never sends His people where He will not sustain them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Contention over water reveals how quickly blessings become battlegrounds. Isaac could have fought, but he yielded the well and called it Esek, "contention." The meekness of the heir of promise stands in stark contrast to grasping, pointing us to the greater Isaac, Jesus, who though Lord of all, chose to give rather than fight for His rights.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again they argue over another well, and he calls it Sitnah, "enmity." Isaac could rightly claim these wells, yet he refuses to repay strife with strife. There is a quiet strength in trusting that the God who made the promise will make room for His people in His own time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At last they dig a well with no quarrel, and Isaac names it Rehoboth, saying, "For now Yahweh has made room for us." After seasons of striving, God's people learn to rest in His timing. The God who blesses also opens doors no man can shut, giving His children space to flourish in His peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the valley of striving Isaac goes up to Beersheba, the place where his father had called on the name of Yahweh. God often draws His weary people back to places of former prayer, reminding them of His faithfulness and inviting them again to worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dark of night, when perhaps Isaac wondered if he would ever be safe, Yahweh appears to him anew. He reminds Isaac of Abraham, but more directly of His own presence: "I am with you." The same God who walked with the fathers walks with His children still, and in Jesus He has promised never to leave us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac's first response to God's renewed promise is worship: he builds an altar and calls on Yahweh's name. Before he digs another well, he digs a place of prayer. The child of faith knows that every blessing flows from communion with the God who gives it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech comes with his friend and his commander, seeking peace. The same people who envied and drove him away now recognize that God is with him. How humbling it is when those who opposed us come asking for covenant with us—not because of our merit, but because of the favor God has shown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac speaks plainly, recalling their hatred and sending him away. He does not pretend, yet he remains open to peace. The believer can be both honest about past wrongs and gracious toward those who now seek reconciliation, trusting the justice and mercy of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They confess what Isaac had already known: "Yahweh was with you." The world may not love God's people, but it cannot deny when the Lord is visibly blessing them. Our greatest witness is not our eloquence, but the peace, kindness, and faithfulness that flow from walking with God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech begs Isaac to swear an oath of peace, acknowledging him as "the blessed of Yahweh." Here is a remarkable reversal: the blessed one is the one they now seek to bless. In Christ, the true Blessed One, those who were once far off are brought near and made blessed together with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac makes them a feast, and they eat and drink together. After years of strife, there is reconciliation around the table. How much greater the feast God has prepared for His enemies who become His friends through the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ!
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They swear to one another and part in peace. Isaac sends them away, not with curses, but with goodwill. The son of promise learns the way of blessing: he refused to repay evil for evil, and now he walks in the peace that comes from trusting God to fight for him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The very same day, Isaac's servants bring him word of another well of water. God's provision comes at just the right time—after the night of promise, after worship, after reconciliation, He gives them water again. Our Father knows what His children need before they ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac names the well Shibah, and the city becomes Beersheba, "well of the oath." The place of strife has become a place of covenant and remembrance. God turns our places of contention into altars of gratitude, reminding us that He has been faithful all the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chapter takes a somber turn: Esau marries two Hittite women. These unions grieve his godly parents, for they reveal Esau's heart more concerned with the present than with the covenant God has given to Abraham's family. Marriage is too weighty to be treated lightly by those who belong to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As readers today, we hear an echo in these grieving hearts. How it grieves our Heavenly Father when we, His children, yoke ourselves to things that are contrary to our identity in Christ. Yet even in such grief, He continues to pursue and restore us by the grace found only in Jesus. As of 2026-10, may we learn to delight in what delights our Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
